extracted.intended_audience: aspiring flash-fiction writers and authors preparing submissions for magazines, small presses, and collections
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing, revising, and submitting flash (micro/sudden) fiction — extremely short stories (typically up to ~1500 words) — including what makes individual pieces and collections publishable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition / word count
rubrics_metrics.description: Flash fiction (microfiction, sudden fiction, short-short, postcard fiction, etc.) runs anywhere from 140 characters to over a thousand words, generally capping out at 1500.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that publishers and contests set their own limits (many prize/series use 500–1,000 words); check target venue guidelines before submitting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compression / conciseness
rubrics_metrics.description: Good flash treats compression as central: 'sharp, tight, and precise' — the form's restraint heightens focus on each language choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid unnecessary words; one unneeded or wrong word can erode reader trust. Note the caveat that 'every word counts' is sometimes a myth — but compression still requires careful word selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language, imagery, and sentence craft
rubrics_metrics.description: Key attributes include language, imagery, rhythm, tone, diction, and excellent sentences — a kind of internal rhythm to the language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize sensory detail and striking imagery; avoid dull or too-familiar words and lazy sentence structure. High-quality sentences can substitute for longer exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surprise / novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: Flash often values surprise and offering something new or different in language, structure, voice, or worldview.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't rely on tired settings/situations/resolutions or go for a twist merely as a gimmick; novelty can be cultural or formal (what is 'good flash' can vary by context and tradition).

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative movement / something happening
rubrics_metrics.description: Difference from a prose poem: in flash there should be 'movement' — something happens or there is a moment of change or transformation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid 'static' pieces that feel inert; even minimal movement or forward motion should propel the piece toward some meaningful change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization / fully formed characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Strong flash situates richly developed characters in a well-delineated setting so readers feel the characters are fully formed people with histories and pasts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imply character depth economically — small details, voice, and action should suggest fuller lives beyond the brief moment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suggestion of a larger context / evoked world
rubrics_metrics.description: Good flash often renders more than a single moment: it suggests a larger world or broader context around the fragment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use implication and selective detail to expand the piece's emotional or situational reach without adding length; beware of pieces that read like truncated scenes from longer works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strong narrative voice / point of view
rubrics_metrics.description: A compelling or distinctive voice can establish character and context efficiently and carry the story's force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop a confident, memorable voice; voice can compensate for limited scope and help the piece feel complete and singular.

rubrics_metrics.name: Title, first line, and last line must work in tandem
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors emphasize three elements: the title, the first line, and the last line — together they have outsized importance in flash.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open immediately (no throat-clearing); make the title arresting; ensure the final line resonates and moves the reader beyond the opening. All three should amplify one another's effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Endings: meaningful closure (avoid dream endings or premature stops)
rubrics_metrics.description: Endings should take the reader somewhere — move beyond where the story began — and avoid cheap devices like 'it was all a dream.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't end too soon; provide a last line that implies consequence or transformation rather than mere description or a nullifying reveal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid reliance on gimmicks, jokes, or extended metaphors
rubrics_metrics.description: A flash piece should not rest on a gimmick, a joke, or a super-long extended metaphor as its primary engine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the story's emotional or narrative core stands independently of any single clever device; novelty alone is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid flabbiness, explanation, and redundancy
rubrics_metrics.description: Common failures include 'flabby' sentences, wasted words, long explanatory passages, and redundancy (clearing the throat).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tighten prose; cut exposition that doesn't advance the piece; eliminate repetitive or superfluous details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid obfuscation; prefer lucid ambiguity
rubrics_metrics.description: It's easy to mistake obfuscation or vagueness for purposeful ambiguity; Chekhov's maxim applies: state the problem correctly and be sharp and lucid in prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be precise even when suggesting rather than explaining; clarity of language makes ambiguity meaningful rather than confusing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative development / avoid mere sketches or scene fragments
rubrics_metrics.description: Pieces that feel like scenes from a longer work, or short stories cut down to meet a word limit, often lack a proper arc or narrative completeness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the piece contains an inherent story (even if compressed) — not just a character sketch or isolated image without a narrative thrust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial publishability checklist (compression, language, character, story, context)
rubrics_metrics.description: From an editor's standpoint, publishable flash comes down to compression, language, character, story, and context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When submitting, assess your piece against these five dimensions: is it concise and precise; is the language compelling; are the characters rendered; is there a story or movement; does it suggest broader context or resonance?

rubrics_metrics.name: Collection-level cohesion and story selection
rubrics_metrics.description: For book-length flash collections, publishers look for cohesion across stories (voice, atmosphere, or recurring elements) and meaningful ordering; each story should matter to the whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open with a super-strong story that sets tone; avoid filler; use ordering and recurring motifs/characters to create accrual of meaning; fewer stronger pieces are better than many mediocre ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial uniqueness / novelty for book publishers
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishers want a collection to offer something singular to the author — not merely mastery of known flash tricks but a distinctive, surprising authorial element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Infuse your work with personal vision or formal inventiveness that distinguishes the manuscript from other flash collections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medium-appropriateness (online vs print considerations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Online magazines often favor very short, bite-sized fiction that suits readers' attention spans; some editors treat flash the same as longer fiction in standards, others emphasize immediacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match the piece's pacing and opening to the venue: prioritize immediate engagement for online markets; still meet core literary standards regardless of medium.
